entry.title: OpenAI: ChatGPT Search Is About 20% of Google's, 250 Million People Speak With ChatGPT, and Chat Is Merging With Work (4 minute read)
entry.content:
OpenAI added 200 million users over just the past two months. Its growth is accelerating. ChatGPT's search volume is approximately 20% of Google's, and its users create 1.5 billion images with it per week. This post contains an edited transcript of an interview with ChatGPT consumer product lead Adam Fry, where he discusses OpenAI's plans to merge ChatGPT's Chat and Work modes, image generation, interactive interfaces, advertising, education, and public unease about AI.

entry.title: The State of Longevity (18 minute read)
entry.content:
The fringe movement of biohackers and people taking a more hands-on approach to longevity has moved into the mainstream thanks to the COVID-19 pandemic and AI chatbots. More and more people are now taking their health into their own hands and spending time, money, and energy on health and longevity. This post looks at how people view health and explores how the people at the cutting edge of health and technology approach their own health. Some of the biggest opportunities in longevity will go to the companies that help people take action and manage their health over time.

entry.title: How software engineering is changing: a tale of two eras (32 minute read)
entry.content:
AI-native startups can ship even faster than fast-moving pre-AI startups because they risk nothing by moving too fast. The old constraints of software engineering have disappeared, allowing startups to move faster, but also break things. The new constraints are too much context switching, losing shared context, tougher pacing, less focus on design, and AI plan limits. Many existing technologies and processes will crack under the change.

entry.title: Interpolative Software (5 minute read)
entry.content:
Interpolative software is code that is solidly within the training distribution of models. It can often be specified with just a few sentences of prompting. Novel software is something that has fundamentally not existed before. Writing novel software with agents is challenging, as they are not trained on the task. Not a lot of software is novel, which is fine, as there is still a ton of value in the interpolative stuff.

entry.title: The Death of the Angel Investor (6 minute read)
entry.content:
The economics of angel investing have shifted. Many investors have realized it's potentially more profitable to raise a fund instead of using their own money. Technology startups now move much faster, and running around grabbing small checks from angels is less palatable than grabbing a pre-seed fund to fund a whole initial round. Also, when angels try to fund a round, they are often pushed out by the valuation game.

entry.title: What Is Quantum Advantage Actually Worth? (9 minute read)
entry.content:
Nearly all roadmaps point to a utility-scale quantum computer being developed around 2030. Despite this, there is little confidence or clarity on how these machines will actually be useful. The consensus is now that they'll first be used for breaking cryptography. The second most concrete answer is to use them to generate simulation data for AI labs' science models. This post looks at how else quantum computing could be applied and where all the revenue will come from.

entry.title: Scaling Git at OpenAI (31 minute read)
entry.content:
OpenAI's monorepo's size and demands increased at a staggering pace over the last year, necessitating a revamp of the AI lab's source control system. Its technical staff built Pando, a new backend for Git repositories optimized for concurrent pushes to many branches and to maximize read throughput. The team implemented the backend without interrupting any engineering work or changing how the team uses Git. Pando cut median push latency in production by nearly 5x, and it now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day.

From TLDR · 2026-11-03 · Programming, Design & Data Science

entry.title: Why Agents Are Soon Only Going to Have 1 Tool (9 minute read)
entry.content:
Agents are collapsing their entire tool catalog into one 'exec' tool. This allows models to write short scripts that chain, combine, and await actions inside isolated sandboxes. Models can now reliably combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass. In the previous standard tool-calling model, agents could only perform single actions, but the exec tool allows them to perform multiple actions.

entry.title: Our organizations are being DDoSed from the inside (6 minute read)
entry.content:
Organizations are losing attention as everyone within is doing something they think is useful, but all that work draws on the same limited capacity to understand, review, and decide. Just because work exists doesn't mean it's the right thing to do. Output is not proof of value. A working implementation only means that something can be built, not that it should be - some changes have negative value.

entry.title: The value of open source (16 minute read)
entry.content:
People open source projects for various reasons. Some do it to build a company or product, others do it performatively, and some ship code just for the love of the game. Open source was never free to copy, and the code was never the moat. AI can remake a product, but it can't provide the rest of the value a company generates. The technology is helping maintainers ship and fix problems faster.

entry.content:

entry.content:

The challenge is in creating the deterministic behavior while retaining the agent's freedom to use the best tools for the job. This post discusses a solution that uses a man-in-the-middle egress proxy that forces behavior by denying actions and forces reactions via automated messages.

entry.title: Making agents fast - what I've learnt over the last 12 months (12 minute read)
entry.content:
Knowing what part of inference a project relies on for speed is important. Check thinking budgets, and read traces, as they often contain valuable insight into what an agent wants to do. Give agents the tools they want rather than what you think they need. Faster hardware still matters, sandboxing and microVMs add complexity, parallelization helps, and classic software performance optimization is still relevant.

entry.title: Unveiling The Grid: PCBs made in America, twice as fast as Shenzhen (3 minute read)
entry.content:

Every board takes its own route through the factory, which has machines that print solder paste, place parts, reflow, solder, and inspect. With The Grid, printing one unit of 100 designs is as easy as printing 100 units of one, and prototypes and production batches run on the same machines. entry.content:
Anthropic asked an internal research model to design mini binders, small proteins that attach tightly to a target, against scorpion neurotoxins as part of its work in experimenting with how Claude can accelerate drug discovery. 17 of the 211 designs tested met Anthropic's criteria. Anthropic has not confirmed whether these binders neutralize scorpion venom in a cellular environment, so it is not claiming to have produced an antivenom. However, the study is a promising first step towards using AI to design credible binders against hard-to-target toxins in days, with lab confirmation within weeks. The challenge, as always, will be turning those binders into safe, affordable, and widely accessible drugs.

entry.title: How To Use Decision Models for Evals (23 minute read)
entry.content:
Decision models are an appealing alternative to LLM judges for automated evals. However, whether they're the right choice depends on the cost, performance, and latency requirements of the use case. Many people leave the default decision threshold at 0.50 without checking whether that's appropriate for the task, leaving a lot of performance on the table. This post shows how to tune thresholds to get the best results from decision models, compares cost and performance between models, and explores how to interpret model scores and how calibration can make them more useful.
